pages.text: Lansing voters changed the city charter in 2025. They wanted a new way to see city money. The city built a Tax and Debt Dashboard. It went live on its August 1 deadline. You can see every tax millage and every bond the city owes on the website. The dashboard shows what people pay and what the city owes.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: However, it does not show everything. It does not show tax breaks for companies. It does not show money the city moves to other projects. It also does not show lawsuits or city contracts. The charter scoped the dashboard to millages and debt. The city followed the rules.

The staff built the page to show exactly what the charter asked for. But some residents want to see more information in one place. Other cities have websites that show more spending details. For now, the dashboard only shows the taxes and the debt.

pages.text: Residents can now easily track the city's debt, including interest rates and payment schedules extending to 2058, without searching through complex audit documents. Despite its utility, the dashboard is limited by its original mandate. It focuses exclusively on what residents are charged and what the city owes.

Consequently, it omits significant financial activities such as tax abatements, diverted tax increments, legal settlements, and vendor contracts. For instance, while the city is considering $6.7 million in tax breaks for apartment complexes, these deals remain absent from the digital tool. City officials note that the dashboard fulfills the specific requirements of Article 7 of the 2026 charter.

The implementing Ordinance #1358 directed staff to create a transparent overview of millages and debt obligations. While other cities like Chicago and New York provide more comprehensive spending data, Lansing’s current tool remains strictly scoped to the parameters set by voters.

pages.text: The Erickson Power Station is now closed. The Board of Water and Light moved the coal ash to a landfill in 2024. However, the ash left pollution in the water. A new report from April 2026 says that lithium is now in the bedrock under the site. The utility company has monitored water for nearby homes since 2022.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: They say the lithium in the bedrock is not in the water people drink. They also say the bedrock at the plant is different from the bedrock under private wells. The company has not yet decided how to clean the site or how much it will cost.
The report shows lithium levels are higher than the rules allow in two deep wells. These wells are at the plant, not in homes. The utility must continue to watch the water and share the results.

keyVocabulary.meaningVi: công ty dịch vụ công ích

evidence: The utility hauled it to a landfill in 2024 .
The lithium has reached the bedrock on the site.
The utility has monitored the water of Delta Township households on private wells near the plant since it found a problem there in 2022.

pages.text: The Board of Water and Light has confirmed that lithium contamination from its retired Erickson Power Station has reached the bedrock beneath the site. Although the utility moved the coal ash to a landfill in 2024, groundwater contamination remains a significant concern.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: A memo from the consultant HDR, dated April 27, 2026, indicates that lithium levels in two bedrock monitoring wells have exceeded established groundwater protection standards for the first time. The utility has been monitoring private wells in Delta Township since 2022 due to previous concerns regarding boron.

In response to the new findings, the company maintains that the contamination is restricted to monitoring wells at the plant and does not affect the deeper aquifer used by local households. However, the utility has yet to select a formal cleanup remedy or provide a cost estimate for the remediation process.

Under federal coal-ash regulations, the utility is required to publish groundwater monitoring results. While lithium levels in shallower glacial groundwater have been documented for years, the recent detection in deeper wells, identified as MW-18C and MW-18D, marks a new development.
These readings are considered health-based cleanup triggers rather than drinking-water standards, as there is currently no enforceable federal limit for lithium in tap water.

headline: Lansing BWL Holds Billion-Dollar Debt

pages.text: The Board of Water and Light (BWL) provides electricity and water to Lansing. Recently, the general manager of the utility, Dick Peffley, spoke to a city council member. He said that the city owns the utility, not the citizens.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: This happened after Council Member Deyanira Nevarez Martinez asked why the utility leader earns more than the U.S. president while rates for customers keep rising. Legally, the city holds the title to the utility. BWL does not have shareholders or a state regulator. All the money it spends comes from the people who pay for electricity, water, and steam.

This money pays for the utility's billion dollars in debt. It also pays for fines and cleanups. On October 1, the bills for customers went up again. BWL has borrowed a billion dollars over 15 years. It never used a competitive bid to get the best price for these loans. Instead, it uses a negotiated method.

This means the utility chooses the bank and the price itself. Customers pay for all of this through their monthly bills. The amount of money from bills that goes toward paying this debt is now rising.

pages.text: Legally, this is accurate; the city acts as a municipal corporation, and the utility is responsible to the Mayor and City Council rather than individual residents. This approach allows the utility to select underwriters and negotiate fees directly. While this method is legal and provides flexibility, it removes the market-based price check that competitive bidding provides. As interest from bond proceeds has been exhausted, a larger portion of every dollar collected from customers is now directed toward servicing this significant debt.

pages.text: This distinction is legally supported by the Lansing City Charter, which establishes the utility as a municipal corporation accountable to the Mayor and City Council. Consequently, BWL operates without the oversight of shareholders or a state regulator, placing the entire financial burden of its operations—including a billion-dollar debt load, regulatory fines, and environmental remediation—squarely upon its ratepayers.

As of June 30, 2025, BWL reported approximately 1.02 billion dollars in long-term debt. Over the past 15 years, the utility has consistently bypassed competitive bidding for its bond issuances, opting instead for negotiated sales. While negotiated deals are a standard practice in public finance, they lack the transparent price discovery mechanism inherent in competitive bidding.

By selecting underwriters directly, the utility retains discretion over terms that are not subject to the rigorous cost-of-capital reviews typically mandated for investor-owned utilities under the Michigan Public Service Commission. The financial implications for residents are significant. With the depletion of capitalized interest from previous bond proceeds, an increasing percentage of utility revenue is now diverted to debt service.

Furthermore, costs associated with non-infrastructure items, such as legal fines and coal-ash cleanup, are integrated into the rate structure without itemization. While BWL maintains investment-grade ratings, the absence of an external price test for its borrowing program leaves ratepayers to absorb the costs of a debt strategy managed entirely through internal appointments and negotiated contracts.

pages.text: With the November 3 election approaching, Representative Tom Barrett has centered his campaign in Michigan's 7th District on the issue of data centers. Mr. Barrett argues that local communities should have the final say over these projects, rather than federal authorities. To support this, he introduced two bills on August 20, 2026, which are currently awaiting committee review.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: The No Data Center NDAs Act (H.R. 10118) aims to prevent members of Congress from signing nondisclosure agreements regarding data center locations or resource usage. Additionally, the Protecting Local Control of Data Centers Act (H.R. 10119) seeks to prevent federal agencies from overriding local zoning decisions. Mr.

Barrett claims that families deserve transparency regarding how these projects impact their utility bills and local environment. Despite his rhetoric, records show that the companies and investors behind these data centers are significant donors to his campaign. Furthermore, the two Michigan utilities that provide electricity to these facilities are also contributors.

When large data centers connect to the grid, state rules often allow utilities to recover infrastructure costs from residential customers, and these agreements are frequently kept from public view. While Mr. Barrett maintains that he is standing up to big corporations, his legislative record includes votes for broader permitting reforms that industry analysts suggest could facilitate data center expansion.

The Protecting Local Control of Data Centers Act (H.R. 10119), cosponsored by other House Republicans, would stop federal agencies from overriding local zoning and siting decisions.

When a large data center connects to the grid, Michigan's rate rules let the utility recover much of the cost of new wires and substations from residential customers, and the contracts that set who pays are often sealed from public view .

pages.text: As the November 3 election draws near, Representative Tom Barrett has positioned data center regulation as a cornerstone of his campaign in Michigan's 7th District. Both bills remain in committee.

The political landscape surrounding these initiatives is complex, as Mr. Barrett’s campaign has received substantial financial support from the very entities he criticizes. This financial overlap is notable given that Michigan’s regulatory framework allows utilities to pass the costs of grid expansion—such as new substations and transmission lines—onto residential ratepayers, often through contracts shielded from public scrutiny. Mr. Barrett’s legislative history reflects a nuanced approach to industry interests.

While he frames his current platform as a challenge to corporate influence, he has previously supported broader permitting reforms, such as the SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), which compresses federal environmental review timelines. Although these votes were not explicitly labeled as data center legislation, reports indicate that such reforms effectively streamline the approval process for the industry. Furthermore, while Mr.

Barrett’s campaign contributions are legally disclosed and common in competitive races, the reliance on corporate PACs and industry-linked donors highlights the tension between his populist messaging and the realities of modern campaign finance.
